item.title: The Fall Hot List
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
At Curated, we have spent the past few months scouting the globe to pinpoint where travel is heading as the leaves turn. We bypassed the tired clichés and the social media noise to bring you the definitive Autumn Hot List—a sharp, editorial lens on the off-the-beaten-path sanctuaries, the emerging cultural pockets, and the tried-and-true classics demanding a second look this season.

Fall travel isn’t about escaping; it’s about leaning into a distinct state of mind. Across our dispatch, two macro movements are dominating the global conversation: Wellness With a Twist and Active Travel. Modern journeys are no longer defined by passive lounging—we want physical presence, restored focus, and deep, immersive energy.

The Big Trends

Wellness with a Twist has taken over the autumn landscape as the classic tropical escape fundamentally pivots away from passive beach lounging toward immersive, culturally driven nourishment. This fall, head to the Caribbean, where low-density shoulder-season travel turns island life into a soulful mental reset. In Dominica, the luxury InterContinental Dominica Cabrits Resort & Spa anchors a warmer, high-energy take on seasonal travel by pairing Cabrits National Park’s waterfalls and hot springs with the vibrant rhythms of October’s World Creole Music Festival. Meanwhile, Antigua and Barbuda Art Week (November 11–18) offers creative renewal through open studios, Flavours & Canvas culinary pairings, and Dual Thresholds—a striking public art installation of 28 reclaimed wooden doors transformed by local artists—proving that real island wellness is as much about artistic vitality as coastal calm.

Active Travel Racquet sports have officially taken over the luxury travel landscape, morphing from a standard amenity into a primary trip driver. The modern journey is built around the court—pairing architectural beauty with competitive movement. Look to the Swiss Alps, where the Valsana Hotel in Arosa delivers high-altitude precision coaching six thousand feet above sea level. Or look to Southeast Asia, where Lombok hosts the region’s very first Rafa Nadal Tennis Center. From private villa courts across Europe to alpine mountain sets, active movement is leading the way.

The Hot List Destinations

Napa Valley, California Harvest season is always Napa’s crown jewel, but this autumn, the valley is reaching a fever pitch. In addition to the hum of early-morning grape picking and the aroma of fermenting cellars, Napa is hosting the landmark Judgment of Napa at Freemark Abbey on October 5th. Commemorating the 50th anniversary of the legendary 1976 Judgment of Paris, this once-in-a-generation blind tasting reunites historic wine icons to pit California’s finest Chardonnays and Cabernets against the world’s best. It makes Napa not just a sensory fall escape, but the absolute epicenter of the international wine world.

Seattle Southside, Washington For a crisp, atmospheric alternative to traditional foliage trips, Seattle Southside is capturing our attention. It seamlessly bridges the gap between vibrant urban culture and raw Pacific Northwest beauty. Think morning hikes along the Puget Sound shoreline and afternoon gallery strolls, followed by hyper-local seasonal food pop-ups that capture the cozy, coastal spirit of the season.

The Isle of Skye, Scotland When summer tourists pack up, Scotland’s Isle of Skye reverts to its wild, poetic roots. The landscape shifts into deep copper and burnished gold, framed by dramatic Atlantic skies and crisp Highland air. Fall here is an exercise in atmospheric luxury: hiking empty trails through ancient glens, gathering around peat fires in local pubs, and soaking in the raw, romantic spirit of the islands in complete quiet.

Andermatt, Switzerland In the quiet window between summer hiking and the arrival of winter ski crowds, Andermatt enjoys a golden, tranquil intermission. Autumn reveals a serene side of mountain living defined by glowing larch forests, clear high-alpine trails, and crisp air. It’s an intimate, design-forward sanctuary for those who want to experience the grandeur of the Alps before the snow falls.

This piece is part of the latest issue of Curated Travel Magazine, where we explore travel through immersive stories, cultural insight, and thoughtfully curated experiences around the world.

item.title: Look Both Ways
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
I didn’t set out to create a magazine. Not really.

One week, I sold $1 million in advertising for the company I worked for. The next, I was laid off for “geopolitical reasons.” In every interview that followed, I heard some variation of the same question: I see you’re analytical, but are you creative? Saying yes was one thing; putting the work on the page was another. So I decided to create something tangible.

I would publish three issues of a travel magazine showcasing my ability to write, edit, and design. Three issues. That was the plan.

But by the time I reached the third, the audience had grown, the responses were rolling in, and I knew I wasn’t going to turn back. Every issue became a love letter...to the industry I spent 20 years promoting, to the art of traveling well, and to the people and places that change us—written with the luxury traveler in mind.

Early in the life of the magazine, I found myself in Miami, a city I’ve visited more times than I can count. But I have a habit when I travel: even in places I know well, I want to find something I haven’t seen before. So I wandered a little farther from the familiar, found a charming little courtyard, ordered a mocktail and settled in to do one of my favorite things—watch people.

And somewhere between the clink of glasses, the passing conversations and the rhythm of the afternoon, it hit me: this is me.

Not that I didn’t already know I loved travel. I had spent 20 years building a career around it. But this felt different. Deeper. The kind of knowing you don’t arrive at through a résumé or a job title. I could feel it in my bones.

Maybe that was what Curated Travel had been becoming all along: not simply a magazine about where to go, but an invitation to look a little closer once you get there.

I stayed up past midnight planning layouts and narrative arcs, researching destinations, and obsessing over the details. I pored over other magazines for inspiration—not just travel, but fashion, food, and, yes, even a decidedly unexpected fishing magazine that somehow made it into the stack.

A year, seven issues, and a frankly absurd amount of iced coffee later, the road hasn’t been without its hurdles.

One of the early hurdles was structural. A major industry platform required a specific format for access. Instead of reshaping the magazine to fit, I built a parallel channel that met the requirement while keeping the editorial standard intact. That channel later became the main route for syndication.

That moment was the pivot point. The accidental experiment stopped being finite and started feeling like a place with its own center of gravity.

I love curating the destination mix, finding the hotels worth highlighting, discovering the stories hiding beneath a place’s obvious attractions—and hearing what you think of the world we’re building here. I’ve learned that some of the best narratives begin in the most unexpected places.

Before you cross the street, you look both ways. So, on this anniversary, I’m taking a moment to look back at where we started—and then forward to wherever we’re headed. To everyone who has subscribed, read, shared, recommended, and wandered through these pages: thank you. You’ve made this possible.

Now, let’s see where we curate next.

This piece is part of the latest issue of Curated Travel Magazine, where we explore travel through immersive stories, cultural insight, and thoughtfully curated experiences around the world.

item.title: oneworld Tackles Jet Lag With Personalized Circadian Science
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Round the World travel may promise the ultimate multi-destination adventure, but crossing multiple time zones can quickly take a toll. Now, oneworld is giving travelers a way to spend less of their journey recovering from jet lag through a new partnership with Timeshifter, a circadian technology company whose jet lag app has been downloaded by more than 1.7 million users.

Effective immediately, travelers booking a Round the World trip through oneworld.com receive a complimentary Timeshifter subscription covering their entire itinerary, from departure through the final return. The personalized program takes into account each flight and time-zone change, along with the traveler’s typical sleep pattern, chronotype and preferences, to recommend when to seek or avoid light and when to sleep. With oneworld’s Round the World trips averaging seven stops and around three months in duration, the partnership addresses one of the less glamorous realities of extended global travel: staying in sync while the itinerary keeps moving.

The Curated Take

For travelers undertaking a true around-the-world journey, time is the luxury. A day spent foggy, exhausted or awake at the wrong hour is a day lost, making circadian planning an unexpectedly valuable addition to the premium travel experience. Rather than treating jet lag as an unavoidable consequence of long-haul travel, oneworld is building recovery and readiness into the journey itself.

item.title: Fusion Brings World Wellness Weekend to Vietnam With Experiences Beyond the Spa
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Fusion is marking World Wellness Weekend, September 18–20, 2026, with a three-day program of complimentary wellness, outdoor and community experiences across its properties in Vietnam. From beachside tai chi and sound healing to herbal workshops, cycling, water sports, healthy cooking and environmental initiatives, the program reflects Fusion’s wellness-inclusive approach while extending beyond the traditional spa experience.

At Fusion Resort & Villas Da Nang, guests can explore sunrise grounding, breathwork, mindful movement and sound-based experiences, while Alba Wellness Valley by Fusion combines meditation, tai chi, outdoor adventures, hot springs and a community charity initiative supporting the Hue Hope Center. Fusion Resort Cam Ranh adds tai chi, herbal and self-care workshops, a community plank challenge and a beach-cleaning initiative. At The Ocean Resort by Fusion Quy Nhon, tennis, kayaking, stand-up paddleboarding, cycling and complimentary water sports encourage guests to experience wellness through movement and the outdoors. In the cities, Grand Royal Riverside Hue - Fusion Collection offers healthy cooking, stretching and morning runs along the Perfume River, while Fusion Suites Vung Tau combines natural-ingredient workshops with charitable giving.

The Curated Take

What makes this program interesting is its breadth. Wellness here isn’t confined to a treatment room or a single type of practice. Guests can move, get outdoors, learn something practical, eat well, care for the environment or simply slow down, while several experiences also invite local communities to participate. For travelers who see wellbeing as part of how they experience a destination, rather than the sole purpose of a retreat, Fusion’s approach offers a more flexible take on the modern wellness getaway.

item.title: In Bali, Bejana and Sababay Pair Two Expressions of Indonesia
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
On September 18, 2026, Bejana by Petty Elliott at The Ritz-Carlton, Bali will bring together two distinctly Indonesian expressions of place for a Sababay Wine Dinner in Nusa Dua. Chef Petty Elliott’s contemporary interpretation of Indonesian cuisine will be paired with wines from Sababay Winery, whose bottles are made in Bali using grapes grown by local farmers in the island’s northern regions.

The evening moves through a menu rooted in the flavors of the archipelago, from sambal teri kacang, tempeh bacam and quail eggs in sambal balado to a coconut and moringa soup, rendang, fish sate lilit and ayam kecap. The pairing continues through dessert, where a pandan and coconut klepon soufflé meets Moscato de Bali. Priced at IDR 1,300,000++ per person, including wine pairings, the dinner offers a particularly intimate way to explore how Indonesia’s culinary traditions and emerging wine culture can meet at the same table.

The Curated Take

For travelers who believe the best way to understand a destination is through its table, this is an appealing Bali experience. Bejana brings together regional recipes and ingredients from across Indonesia, while Sababay offers a taste of the island’s increasingly distinctive winemaking story. Together, they turn a wine dinner into something more meaningful: a portrait of Indonesia told through flavor, farming and local craftsmanship.

item.title: Chester Prepares to Shout Its Way to the World Town Crier Championship
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
“Oyez! Oyez!” will ring through the historic streets of Chester this September as the World Town Crier Tournament returns to the Cheshire city for the first time since 2014. From September 22–26, 2026, 25 town criers representing eight nations, including England, Australia, Canada, Belgium, Germany, the Netherlands, the Channel Islands and the USA, will compete for the title of the world’s best. The free event unfolds across three competition days, with criers judged on vocal power, clarity, showmanship and audience engagement.

The spectacle is particularly at home in Chester, where the tradition of the town crier dates to at least 1554. Competitors in colorful costumes and commanding voices will perform against the city’s Roman walls and distinctive black-and-white medieval architecture, while visitors can explore the Roman Walls, the medieval galleries of The Rows and Chester Cathedral between events. The competitions take place September 22 at Town Hall Square, September 24 at Eastgate Square and September 26 at Exchange Square, with sessions from 11 a.m.–12:30 p.m. and 2–3:30 p.m. each day.

The Curated Take

There is something wonderfully theatrical about encountering a centuries-old tradition still being performed in the heart of a modern city. Chester’s town criers are more than ceremonial performers: they connect visitors to a time when a powerful voice was one of the most important ways to share news. For travelers drawn to places where history remains part of everyday life, a free afternoon of international town-crier competition could be one of the most memorable ways to experience Chester.

item.title: Detroit’s Murals Turn the City Into an Open-Air Art Guide
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Detroit has long been associated with automobiles and Motown, but its creative identity is also written across the city’s walls. With more than 730 murals throughout Detroit and Metro Detroit, public art offers travelers a different way to explore the city, moving beyond the downtown core into neighborhoods where murals reflect local history, cultural identity and community pride. From Southwest Detroit and Corktown to Eastern Market, Milwaukee Junction and Hamtramck, the artwork becomes a kind of unofficial city guide.

In Southwest Detroit, murals explore the area’s Mexican-American and immigrant heritage, while Corktown’s portraits celebrate the people who give Detroit’s oldest neighborhood its character. Downtown’s Belt combines colorful urban art with nightlife, and Eastern Market’s murals complement one of the city’s most vibrant food destinations. Further afield, Milwaukee Junction connects contemporary street art with Detroit’s history of innovation, while murals in the North End and Hamtramck explore the city’s Black music legacy and immigrant communities. Highlights include Sydney G. James’s Girl with a D Earring, Hebru Brantley’s Fly Boys and Dasic Fernandez’s Yemen Mural. An interactive mural map from the City of Detroit makes it possible to build a self-guided route around the artwork.

The Curated Take

Detroit’s murals are most interesting when viewed as more than colorful backdrops. They offer travelers a way to understand the neighborhoods themselves, revealing stories of immigration, music, cultural heritage, resilience and reinvention that aren’t always visible from the city’s major attractions. For visitors willing to follow the art outward from downtown, a mural hunt becomes an unexpectedly intimate introduction to Detroit.

item.title: Four Seasons Chiang Mai Welcomes New General Manager Ivan Giles
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Four Seasons Resort Chiang Mai and Four Seasons Tented Camp Golden Triangle have appointed hospitality veteran Ivan Giles as General Manager, bringing more than two decades of international experience across luxury resorts in the Americas and Asia to the two Northern Thailand properties. Giles joins from Four Seasons Resort Langkawi, where he led the resort through a period of repositioning, villa enhancements and record business performance, including the distinction of two Michelin Keys.

A longtime Four Seasons leader, Giles began his career in Mexico before joining the company in Costa Rica in 2004, going on to hold leadership roles in destinations including Hawaii, the Maldives and Malaysia. His new role brings him to Chiang Mai’s rice fields and mountains, where he will oversee both properties and focus on deepening connections between guests, local communities and the region’s Lanna culture. He also takes the helm of the Tented Camp Golden Triangle, with its more adventurous, nature-focused approach to Northern Thailand.

The Curated Take

Giles’ appointment comes at an interesting moment for Northern Thailand, where luxury hospitality increasingly revolves around a strong sense of place rather than simply polished accommodations. His experience guiding resorts through transformation, combined with his emphasis on people and community, could make his arrival particularly relevant for travelers seeking experiences that feel connected to the destination rather than simply set within it.

item.title: When Skiing Ability Stays but Confidence Fades
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
For some experienced skiers, the problem isn’t ability. It’s nerve. VIP SKI is putting a rarely discussed part of the ski experience in focus with its new Ski Confidence Reset and a dedicated Ski Confidence Week in Val d’Isère in April 2027, designed for skiers who still know how to ski but no longer feel quite as confident doing it. An injury, time away from the mountains, pressure to keep pace with family or friends, or simply becoming more conscious of the consequences of a fall can all change the experience.

Developed with Kate Casali, The Ski Mindset Coach®, the program combines traditional instruction with mindset coaching. Guests begin with a confidential questionnaire and individual pre-trip session, followed by ski instruction with Oxy Ski School, group confidence work, individual coaching and an introduction to Emotional Freedom Technique (EFT) in Val d’Isère. A post-holiday session helps participants reflect on what has changed. The goal isn’t to make skiers fearless or push them onto more challenging terrain, but to help them reconnect with skills they already possess. The seven-night April 11, 2027 stay at No 6 Bellevarde starts from £1,268 per person based on two sharing, including chalet board, the confidence program, ski guiding and group Geneva transfers.

The Curated Take

There’s an interesting honesty to admitting that skiing can change even when your technique hasn’t. For families, couples and longtime ski travelers, confidence can quietly become the difference between joining the group for another run and opting for lunch instead. VIP SKI’s approach recognizes that getting people back on the mountain may require something different from another lesson: sometimes the most useful skill to relearn is trusting yourself.

item.title: At Four Seasons The Nam Hai, Sustainability Starts in the Garden
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
At Four Seasons Resort The Nam Hai, Hoi An, sustainability is becoming less of a behind-the-scenes initiative and more of something guests can see, taste and experience. The resort has earned its second consecutive EarthCheck Silver Certification for a sustainability approach that connects environmental stewardship with cultural preservation and community engagement. Nearly 80 percent of the 35-hectare property is devoted to gardens and green spaces, including a regenerative herb and vegetable garden that supplies the resort’s restaurants, bars and spa with ingredients ranging from butterfly pea flowers and sugarcane to papaya, kale and dragon fruit.

That garden is part of a larger closed-loop system that processes more than 1,000 tons of organic material each year into compost, while other initiatives recycle cooking oil and glass, reuse landscaping materials and reduce single-use packaging. Guests can participate through garden walks, planting activities and garden-to-table cooking classes, as well as cultural experiences that support local artisans and traditions. Beyond the resort, scholarship programs invest in education, while the Adopt a Tree, Restore the Riverbank initiative supports native tree planting along the Thu Bồn River. Upcoming biodiversity efforts, including a beehive program, will further extend the property’s environmental focus.

The Curated Take

The most interesting part of The Nam Hai’s sustainability story is how little of it feels separate from the luxury experience. The same garden that supports biodiversity supplies ingredients for dinner and treatments at the spa; cultural preservation becomes something guests can experience firsthand; and environmental restoration gives travelers a way to participate rather than simply observe. It is a useful model for what responsible luxury can look like when sustainability is woven into the fabric of a stay rather than presented as a separate program.
